subtopic: PACIFIC HALIBUT FISHERY
PACIFIC HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
1.	Is it the intention of the government to introduce to this house a bill confirming the treaty for securing the preservation of the halibut fishery of the north pacific ocean, which was made between His Majesty the King and the United States of America and which was signed at Washington on March 2, 1924, and ratified by His Majesty on October 21, 1924, and authorizing the government of Canada to perform the obligations therein imposed upon the Dominion of Canada?
2.	If not, why not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PACIFIC HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
may I draw the attention of my hon. friend to what appears to be the effect of the second question he asks, in each of the questions he has put before the house: I refer to the "if not, why not"? And in that connection may I read the rule of the house, standing order No. 44:
Questions may be placed on the order paper seeking information from the ministers of the

Questions
crown relating to public affairs; and from other members l elating to any bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the business of the house, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same. And in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that if the government were to attempt to answer the question "If not, why not", we might be drawn into the realm of argument with my hon. friend. There is no desire on the part of the administration not to give my hon. friend the fullest information possible. I can at the proper time supply him with the reasons that have governed in these matters, I shall be glad to give them to him at any time if he so desires, but in answering the question I think the nde of the house just quoted should be observed and that the same rule should be observed with respect to answers to my honourable friend's questions as will be followed with all hon. members of the house. Later on it will be seen there are other questions similarly worded, I am going to ask in each case to be allowed to take exception to answering the question "If not, why not". With that exception, I have here the answers to all of my hon. friends questions.

subtopic: PACIFIC HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
Does Your Honour rule
that the question "If not, why not", necessarily provokes discussion?

subtopic: PACIFIC HALIBUT FISHERY
speechtext:
The rule is very clear.
In the putting of questions, or replying to same, no argument or opinion is to be offered. The purpose of a question which is placed on the order paper is to secure information as to plain matters of fact, and no discussion may arise therefrom. I would rule that the words "If not, why not" are out of order. Questions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 are answered, I understand, provided the words "If not, why not" are deleted from the questions.

The rule that has just been cited, Mr. Speaker, makes it clear that a question should not be asked in that way. I might draw the attention of the hon. member to what is further implied in the rule. Beauchesne's Rules and Forms, section 342:
A question which publishes the names of persons or statements not strictly necessary to render the question intelligible will be refused a place on the notice paper.
There are statements in the question that has been asked that are not at all necessary to render it intelligible, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, they should not have a place on the order paper. I would also direct my hon. friend's attention to section 349:
The purpose of a question is to obtain information and not to supply it to the house. A question may not contain statements of facts unless they be necessary to make the question intelligible and can be authenticated; nor should a question contain arguments, inferences, imputations, epithets or controversial or ironical expressions.
I do not know how many of those last mentioned characteristics are to be found in my hon. friend's question, but certainly there are enough of them to justify the government in refusing to make reply to it in its present form.

speechtext:
1.	What success has attended the grading of beef in Canada?
. 2. How many stores are handling graded beef in each of the cities, Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal?
3.	What percentage of beef suitable for grading is being graded?
4.	hat is being done to encourage producers m supplying a regular supply of quality beef suitable for grading?

6.	How do stocks of fresh killed Canadian lamb in storage on January 1, 1930, compare with stock on hand on January 1, 1929?
/. What steps are the Canadian government taking to secure a share of the British bacon an^ thereby help to establish greater stability m prices, more confidence among producers, and an expansion in the swine industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: GRADING AND STORAGE OF MEATS
speechtext:
1.	While official grading of beef has been in effect in Canada for only five months and must, therefore, be regarded as more or less in the experimental stage, it has met with a very encouraging response and its success so far has been most gratifying.
2.	As the number of stores handling graded beef is increasing almost daily in order to meet the steadily growing demand for graded beef, it is impossible to state the exact number at present handling this product. In the cities mentioned, many of the foremost dealers, including some of the larger chain stores, are now featuring officially graded beef and some

of them are handling it exclusively. Incidentally it must be stated that about ten days ago a report was received by the Department of Agriculture to the effect that over seventy stores were handling graded beef in the city of Winnipeg including Hudson Bay and the T. Eaton Companies.
3.	Some establishments are branding all beef which is eligible; others are branding upon order only. The percentage branded varies according to the fluctuations between supply and demand.
4.	The development of production programs to increase the supply of young unfinished cattle is under way in several of the provinces. The activities of provincial committees which are in process of organization in this connection, are being coordinated by federal officers with a view to furthering the campaign already under way to assure an adequate and constant supply of beef suitable for grading. A production campaign for finished cattle is also being arranged for the exhibition circuits and western feeder shows, as well as through other channels, and proper feeding and finishing methods are being encouraged through the direct field work of federal officials and by special and carlot classes for such cattle which have been arranged for at various fairs.
5.	Lamb in storage January 1, 1930, 8,261,694 pounds; lamb in storage Janauary 1, 1929, 5,967,946 pounds.
6.	Lamb in storage not frozen January 1, 1930, 299,644 pounds; lamb in storage not frozen January 1, 1929, 222,218 pounds.
7.	The hog grading policy has achieved its object to place on the British market a quality of product equal to the best imported product offered and it has narrowed the spread of price to a very favourable margin. The improvement in the quality of our hogs has however stimulated domestic consumption to the point where 95 per cent or over is sold at home. Since 1921, our consumption has increased by 6 pounds per capita. Also a rapidly expanding tourist trade is absorbing a very large percentage of the annual surplus. Our total production in 1929 was fairly well in line with the five year average. Unfortunately just at present home consumption seems to have gone ahead of production and no bacon is being exported from Canada this calendar year.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the setting up of a system of intermediate credits for agriculture.
He said: In discussing this question of agricultural credits an international authority used this method of illustration:
"The use of credit in agriculture may be compared to the use of water. If the water is brought into the field at the right time in the proper way and in proper quantities it will prove invaluable, but if the field is flooded or if the water is applied at the wrong time it will be destructive."
I shall attempt to discuss this subject from that point of view, Mr. Speaker, realizing that
300	COMMONS
Agricultural Credits-Mr. Speakman
credit overdone or used to too great an extent or in an improper manner, is more likely to defeat the object sought than to bring it into effect. All of those-and I imagine that includes most members of this house-who are familiar with agriculture and who have considered the subject of credits as applied to agriculture, recognize that there are three distinct phases, or methods of using credits, three distinct fields of agricultural credits. The first is that covered by the term "long term credits". Up to a short time ago that field was covered mainly, and indeed wholly, by the different mortgage companies who loaned money for various purposes on the security of the land. The distinction which might be drawn between the three forms of credit, which generally have been recognized as long term, short term, and intermediate, depends on three distinct factors. They are the term of years for which the money is loaned, the security which is asked and the purpose to which that money is devoted. In the case of long term credits the only security asked or accepted is the security of the land mortgaged, the reason obviously being that land alone, of all agricultural property, is not subject to change or fluctuation or to serious depreciation. It is there at all times, and always' possesses a certain value which renders it a proper form of security. The purpose for which the money is used under the long term form is, as a general rule, either for the purchase of land, for the renewing of existing indebtedness on more favourable terms, or for the erection of permanent improvements which, being of major value and permanent in character, should be paid for over the long term of years during which they retain their full measure of usefulness.
I might point out before I enter upon my subject proper that it was only after years of discussion and consideration that we took the final step in this country to place the Canadian farmer in a situation comparable to that occupied by farmers in most other countries by providing him with a form of credit suitable to his needs in that respect. It is too early at this stage, Mr. Speaker, to say with any degree of certainty or definiteness just how successful that attempt has been. We are still in the experimental stages. We do not know just how far the system of long term farm loans, our federal farm loans which we have inaugurated will prove satisfactory to the farmers w'ho will use the credit thus supplied, and that being the case it would be premature for me to pass any definite opinion upon what has occurred. I simply say this, that in the case of this act as in the case of most other acts, and in the case of this scheme 
as in the case of most other schemes, certain weaknesses have become apparent-weaknesses to which I will refer very briefly a little later on- and for the remedying of which I propose to offer certain suggestions.
Since Canada became a nation, we have had a system of short term loans, familiarly termed bank loans, and up until but recently, and in the field which I propose to discuss even at the present time, it is the only form of loan which is acceptable to the farmer or to any other person. It has been the experience not only of farmers but of bankers and business men that the loans provided by the banks under the system which they must follow, under the conditions which must be imposed, are neither suitable for the purpose of agriculture nor do they meet the need which obviously exists. The reason for that is two or three fold. In the first place, the time for which the money may profitably be loaned by any bank is too short for it to be of any great value to the agriculturalists although undoubtedly it is suitable to many forms of commercial activity. I have no criticism at all to offer of our banking system; it was designed and has proven suitable to ordinary merchandising and ordinary commercial life, but the very conditions under which the money is loaned, the very terms upon which it is advanced are obviously suited only to that kind of business where the turnover takes place very frequently and at short intervals. In agriculture the obverse is the case. Even with the most successful farmer, the farmer who is so happily situated in regard to climate, in regard to soil, in regard to his own abilities, as to secure a crop once every year, cannot by any stretch of the imagination have more than an annual turnover. Twelve months must elapse even under the most happy conditions between one crop and another. It is obvious therefore, that a loan which can profitably be advanced only for a term of three months, with possible renewal for six months, cannot under any conceivable stretch of imagination meet the case.
Another point which renders this form of credit of very little value to the farmer is this. Owing to the fact that the return received, on the most happily situated farms, is so moderate, the interest rates charged by the average bank are too high to enable- that money to be used with any degree of advantage. We have provided for the farmer who wishes to borrow money for long terms up to 25 or 35 years to be used for certain specific purposes. In our banking system we have ready access, provided the security can be offered, to credit for certain short terms

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Speakman
and temporary purposes but, as I have stated, that is of very little use to the farmer, although he can and does make use of bank credit in some instances. For example, he may borrow money from the bank for the purchase of seed, hoping that within six months or so his crop will have matured and he will be able to repay the loan. He may borrow money for the purpose of buying feed for the same length of time. He may borrow for the purpose of paying his taxes in order to keep himself in good standing in the municipality and to avoid the penalities which are attached to delay in the payment of taxes. He may borrow for various temporary purposes to meet temporary necessities, but there is one class of farmer of great and of increasing importance for whom no adequate provision has been made, and that is the farmer who is anxious to go into mixed farming. the man who is anxious to build up and develop a dairy herd or to purchase young stock for the purpose of maturing and fattening that stock and placing it upon the market at the most favourable time and under the best possible conditions. To him a bank loan is of little value, and indeed the experience in the past of stock owners, those men who build up dairy herds or who buy young stock for the purpose of marketing at a latex date, has not been happy.
I may say-using the personal note moment-arily_that I am one of those men who from time to time have handled stock. Personally I have not been faced with the neccess-ity of borrowing money for that purpose, but I have seen farmers in my neighbourhood and I know of farmers throughout the whole province and the whole of Canada who have been so unfortunate as to incur that indebtedness. With what result? This was the result that followed almost invariably and which resulted in the partial bankruptcy and sometimes in the total ruin of those men. They borrowed a sum of money, adequate as they thought for their needs, with the assurance of the bank that the}7 would be able to renew the note from time to time as necessity demanded. But with the fluctuations in the market, very frequently the banks called their loans at a time when the stock was not matured, or not fit for the market, or when the market itself was not in a receptive condition, and they were faced with one or the other of these two alternatives. They were forced to put the unfinished stock on the market and take what they could, with a certain loss of money, or they were forced to borrow from some other quarter in order to meet the deficiency. The inevitable result was this: many of those men,
who in good faith entered into the business of stock raising or the preparing of stock for the market, found themselves forced to dispose of that stock prematurely and approached bankruptcy through the losses which they incurred.
Those of us who have been familiar with this situation, and who believe as I believe that stock farming is and should be a permanent and important part of our agricultural system throughout Canada, believe that we should have a system of credit which would be particularly suited to that particular industry, a system of credit under which money could be borrowed in reasonable quantities and under strict business principles, but which would be devoted to the purpose of purchasing young stock and which would be available for that purpose until that stock could be matured to advantage. If that were done, we believe that the business of raising stock, the mixed farming which we believe will be more and more the basis of successful agriculture, will again come to the front as a flourishing, important and profitable branch of this industry.
Now, what suggestions have we to offer and in what way has this situation been met in other countries? I am mentioning other countries for one reason above all others. In Canada we have been watching developments in that great country to the south and there we have found not only that the importance of agriculture has been fully realized, but that governments, both federal and state, municipalities, banks and all other financial organizations, have placed at the command of the agriculturist almost unlimited credit to be used for his particular industry. The United States has set aside vast sums of money to enable the farmers, if possible, to get on their feet and place themselves in a more fortunate position than that which they at present occupy. Indeed, to me it has been an occasion for pride that to a very great degree the Canadian farmer has been doing for himself, and asking for no governmental assistance in it, things which the United States farmer has looked to his government to provide for. The Canadian farmer, at his own expense and on his own initiative, has inaugurated marketing systems, which, in spite of temporary setbacks, in spite of adverse marketing conditions, will, I believe, place him upon a much firmer basis in the future than that which he has occupied in the past. In many lines of endeavour our farmers are showing themselves full of initiative, independence, and ready to do for themselves what they can do instead of asking for governmental assistance.

speechtext:
I was just coming to
that. The next point is the security to be offered, for as I indicated at the opening of my remarks, the differences between these various forms of credit can be classified under three heads: (1) the term of years for which the money shall be loaned, the long term loan being limited to a maximum period of some thirty-five years, and the short term loan being limited to from three to six months; and for intermediate credits we suggest a term of from six months up to three or possibly five years; (2) the class of security which is demanded. In the case of long term credits, land is the only security accepted. In the case of bank credit the personal note and the personal obligation of the borrower, backed and seconded by the endorsement of some other dependable person, who would in turn assume his obligation, is the security usually asked for. In the case of intermediate credits, the security always demanded is a chattel mortgage on the stock itself, supplemented by other chattels of a marketable character.
Naturally and obviously in lending this money, strict business principles must be applied, and for the sake of the farmer of the country, of the institution which lends the money, no more money should be loaned than may be adequately secured by an approved form of security. I am not one of those who believe that the lavish expenditure of money, the wide-open power to borrow in any amount regardless of security and of the use to which the money is to be put, is a good thing for anybody. But I do think that credit wisely applied and judiciously extended is the very lifeblood of all business though in this case, as in the case of all other countries where the system is applied, the security is the chattel mortgage upon the stock purchased, supplemented by chattel mortgages upon other marketable security of a class which will not deteriorate too rapidly.
The purpose for which it would be applied would be, as I have indicated, the purchase
of young or dairy stock with the object in view either of building up a dairy herd or of maturing and fattening that stock, and placing it upon the market at the best possible time and in the best possible condition.
I have indicated, then, the terms, the life of the loan, the security, and the general purpose which I have in view. I am asking that this subject shall be sympathetically considered. I have intimated that in my opinion the best place for its proper consideration would be the banking and commerce committee, and I suggest that when the subject is being considered by that committee it consider also the question of long term credits, the functioning of the present act, and the various complaints which have arisen from time to time, together with the possibility of some improvement in the regulations. I have said that I am ready and willing to accept an amendment to that effect to bring about the reference of the question to a committee; and assuring the house that I have not brought the matter before it without realizing what it means, without realizing the dangers and the difficulties which an injudicious use of credit might bring in its train, I would urge that this proposal be considered sympathetically in the hope that some system of credit suited to agriculture, and suited particularly to the stockmen and mixed farmers of this country, may be provided and put into force.

speechtext:

an amendment that the matter be referred to the banking and commerce committee, as there is no specific mention in the resolution of the method to be employed in giving the consideration which I ask.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): I think both the substance and form of the presentation by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) of this subject of intermediate credits merited far more attention than they received. I confess that I had some difficulty in following him because of the difficulty in hearing all that he said.
I gathered, however, that the hon. member traversed the ground in connection with what is sometimes called the blank spot in agricultural credit; that is, that area between the short-term credit, well provided under the terms of the Bank Act, and as extended by the chartered banks of the country, and, at the other extreme, the long-term land mortgage system. In between, as my hon. friend states, is the problem of supplying the kind of credit on chattle security adapted for various forms

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Dunning
of agriculture, and particularly for the industry of stock raising. The subject has been studied at various times on behalf of Canada, the last report being, I believe, that of Doctor Tory, which was made available in 1924 and out of which grew the long term farm loan system which is now in operation. The Canadian farm loan system has been in operation now for several months. Loans have already been placed, I believe, in six of the provinces, and under the terms of the act approximately $1,608,000 has been loaned.
My hon. friend made reference to the developments which have taken place in this connection in the United States. It will be remembered that, following many years of study by numerous commissions the United States finally adopted what might be called a comprehensive agricultural credit system, changing in some respects their method of dealing with short-term credits for agriculture as well as with intermediate and long-term credits. Experiments in this connection have been going on for several years. Although perhaps it is a little too early yet to state just what the results are in the United States, so far as the successful operation and attainment of the objective is concerned, I have some information here regarding the operation of intermediate credit institutions in that country which might be of use to the house at this juncture.
Under the system which was evolved as the result of years of inquiry in the United States, there was included the establishment of twelve intermediate credit banks. They were established in the same cities as the federal land banks, and were set up as separate corporations, although having the same officers and boards of directors. Each of these intermediate credit institutions had a capital stock of $5,000,000, entirely subscribed by the government of the United States. These institutions also have power to issue debentures up to ten times the amount of the paid-up capital and surplus, the security to be cash, or paper representing loans. In the case of these United States intermediate credit organizations the method of doing business is not directly with the farmer. The loans are made from the twelve national intermediate credit institutions through the medium of state or national banks, trust companies, agricultural credit corporations, incorporated live stock loan companies, savings institutions, cooperative banks, cooperative marketing associations of agricultural producers, or other federal intermediate credit banks. That sounds rather complex, but my point is that the federal intermediate credit system of the United States

operates by discounting the paper of other institutions, and not by discounting the paper of the farmer direct.
I have here a diagram from Doctor Tory's report indicating the relationship of the various unit parts of the United States scheme, and in that connection I note that a form of joint stock land bank was established as part of the intermediate credit system of the United States, having a direct relationship with the federal farm loan board. Eighty joint stock banks were provided for, with a capital of $250,000 each. I understand that this part of the United States' development in connection with agricultural credit has not been so successful in operation as the other portions of the system; or perhaps it would be fairer to say that weaknesses have developed in connection with joint stock land banks to a greater degree than they have become apparent in the other branches of the system. For instance, three of the joint stock land banks have been placed in receivership with outstanding liabilities of more than $70,000,000, namely, the Kansas City Joint Stock Land Bank, Kansas city, Missouri, the Bankers Joint Stock Land Bank, Milwaukee, and the Ohio Joint Stock Land Bank, Cincinnati. The fact that these institutions are in difficulties, however, does not necessarily mean that the whole structure is inadequate or inefficient, and it does not mean that the twelve intermediate credit institutions set up under the same authority are in any difficulty. But it is a little too early for us to say that the institutions evolved by the United States as a result of their exhaustive inquiry are yet past the experimental stage. I think my hon. friend from Red Deer who has given some study to this matter will agree with that statement.
It is important that we should profit by the mistakes of our neighbours, whatever they may be. I am more concerned with profiting by their mistakes than I am with following their example along many lines. In this regard allow me to quote from a report of a study of recent economic changes made in the United States in 1929. This study was undertaken by a national committee, not any voluntary organization, with Herbert Hoover, now President of the United States, as the head of it. The remarks made in connection with the credit situation as it affects agriculture are, I think, particularly useful to us in this discussion. Mr. Hoover's committee says, and, remember, this is in 1929, quite recently:

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Dunning
Many rural districts were inadequately served with credit in the years shortly before the World war when the rural credit agitation first came to an acute stage. With the passing of the Federal Reserve act, the Federal Farm Loan act, and the Intermediate Credit act, the way had been paved for the removal of many difficulties; though obviously no mere passing of legislation can create a desired volume of credit, or suitable administration of its extension. In practice, "sympathetic" officials in some of these institutions have extended lines of credit involving losses of some magnitude. These losses, however, will doubtless be absorbed in our structure without serious harm, distributing scarcely avoidable losses to shoulders more able to bear them than those on which they originally fell.
The main point, however, is how the extension of credits is to be suitably adjusted to the productive organization of our agriculture in the future.
That is significant as indicating that the United States do not yet regard their system as working perfectly or even satisfactorily. The report goes on:
Perhaps we may grant in a broad way that the several pieces of rural credit legislation already enacted have tended to put the credit resources of the country at the disposal of the agricultural industry upon terms as advantageous as those available to other industries and adapted to the peculiar requirements of the business and those who are engaged in it. We must not. however, put the cart before the horse. Adequate credit facilities will not create a satisfactory credit situation for agriculture, but on the other hand a satisfactory basis of credit must precede the extension of loans.
That is the precise difficulty that the United States scheme is meeting in operation, the finding, not of the money to loan, but of a satisfactory basis upon which to extend the loan; which is of course a fundamental problem in connection with any credit scheme. The report continues:
Even those farmers who in the years just following the war laid stress on the ability of liberal credit extension to serve them in the deflation period have seen the limitations of such relief measures and have coined the phrase "You can't borrow yourself out of debt."
That is all I wish to quote from the report, merely by way of giving information to the house how sympathetically official United States' opinion regards the experiment which has been conducted in that country and the operation of it.
So far as Canada is concerned, we could of course approach the matter from the point of view of enlarging the powers of the chartered banks to take security. We could, if we wished-personally I doubt the wisdom of it -permit our chartered banks to take classes of security which would enable them to enter more largely into what is known as the inter-2419-20
mediate credit field. In fairness to our banks,
I think it should be said that although not having the power to take the kind of security which is taken in other countries, our chartered banks do in fact materially facilitate the very operation of live stock production and so forth which we are discussing, and which require in reality a longer term of credit than the ordinary three month note. But I doubt very much, Mr. Speaker, if this house would care to go on record as considering it desirable that there should be a widening of the security-taking powers of our chartered banks along this line. The criticism of course is that to the extent to which banks do tie up their funds in long term loans their position is thereby rendered less liquid. And I have the old fashioned idea of a bank; its first essential should be that it is a safe place in which to put money; its lending features are secondary from my point of view. Unless it is a safe place to deposit money it will not last long as a bank. And to the extent that we permit the tying up of deposits for longer periods than prevail under the present law, to that extent we are opening the possibility at least that depositors might not be able to get their money out on demand.

speechtext:
There was no rural
credit legislation. That is a distinction which I want to draw. Rural credits, as I understand it, is a broad term which includes lending of all kinds to rural people; that is to say, it includes any system of short term lending, of intermediate lending, and of long term farm mortgages. This parliament, I would say to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) dealt with just one phase of that in its legislation enacted, I think, in 1926. The one phase which this parliament dealt with then was the long term mortgage credit phase of the problem.
The phase we are now discussing is different entirely. In the United States, as I have indicated, separate organizations are created for intermediate credit. True, they are under the same general management, but I submit it would be impossible for such institutions to be under the same general management as long term credit organizations if the intermediate credit organization were itself dealing directly with the farmer. The fact that the twelve intermediate banks in the United States are dealing, not with the farmer, but with the other organizations, which in their turn dis-



Agricultural Credits-Mr. Dunning
count the farmers' paper, renders it possible and practicable for the administration of the intermediate credit bank to be the same as that of the federal farm loan institution. There is a wide field for speculation as the manner of dealing with the actual administration of such an organization. In the United States the organization does not itself deal directly with the farmer but with organizations of various kinds which in turn deal with the farmer. The intermediate credit organization discounts the paper of various types of organization which, under the law, deal with the farmer with respect to the credit, and are in the first instance responsible for so doing. Therein lies a very important aspect of the problem. The United States farmer who borrows under the facilities provided by the intermediate credit portion of their farm loan legislation deals with some local organization which is wholly responsible for dealing with him. The intermediate credit institution has nothing whatever to do with the individual farmer. It does not lend money to the individual farmer, does not realize upon the security, if it is necessary to realize upon it; but the local organization is able to send that farmer's paper in as an individual piece of paper to combine *with all the rest of its loans of a similar class to the intermedia te credit institution and borrow itself on the amount of paper discounted en bloc. In Canada it would be rather difficult to organize in such a way, as I think my hon. friend from Red Deer will appreciate. Our conditions are different, and there are many parts of the United States from which complaints on that ground are coming at the present time, the ground being that the situation of the people in many parts of the United States does not permit of the establishment of the initial institution through which the discounting is conducted that it is difficult for them to create the kind of institution which can qualify as a discounting organization under the terms of the intermediate credit legislation by borrowing from one of the twelve intermediate credit banks.
I did not intend to go on at length in connection with this matter, Mr. Speaker,-

Referring to the question asked by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I do not think the minister has answered it as I had expected he would. He asked whether the present system of long term rural credits did not go to relieve the situation. He referred to stock raising. As I understand it, if a man has a farm free of mortgage he can go to this board
IMr. Dunning.]
and get a long term rural credit for the purpose of raising stock, or doing anything else in connection with the improvement of the farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
I am sorry I did not get the point my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre was making. The legislation which passed this house in 1026, being now in operation, contributes in some measure toward the supplying of funds to farmers for stock raising, provided	the	farmer has	real	estatesecurity to offer and is in a position to take a long term loan for it. In actual practice- and I speak	as an individual	who	raisesstock-if a man is really thrifty in his farming operations he	does	not regard	it as	goodbusiness to take out	a thirty-year	loan for the
purpose of financing the growing of stock which must, of necessity, come to maturity, if it is to be profitable, in three years.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Surely he is not obliged to take out a thirty-year loan. He can take a shorter loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Not under the terms of the federal farm loan scheme which passed this house. It is a long term loan system.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Surely that cannot be the case. Can he not take it for a shorter term?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
Is there not a provision
in the bill whereby the loan can be repaid after five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS

speechtext:
If I may interrupt again, I am quite sure that this particular purpose was considered when the farm loan act was passed, and that a thrifty farmer who

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Dunning
wished to increase his stock, or do anything else in connection with his farm which would be spread over several years, could come to this board for a loan and use it for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Oh, undoubtedly.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: If he had to keep it for thirty years, there is something wrong with the act. I am quite sure the minister is mistaken that he cannot get it for a shorter term. In fact, I am sure that that was one of the purposes for which the act was passed.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
I can assure my hon.
friend that he cannot get a short term loan from the board, but he undoubtedly has the power of repayment.
Sir GEORGE PERLEY': That is the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
But that does not convert a farm loan scheme into an intermediate credit scheme. That is the distinction I am trying to draw, which my hon. friend from Red Deer referred to in his own remarks. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, I am not at the present time indicating that, in my judgment, Canada can approach this problem from the point of view of setting up a new organization for the purpose of developing intermediate farm credits immediately. I do not think that there is yet sufficient experience on this continent in the working either of long term farm mortgage loans, organized as ours is under federal law, or of intermediate credit loans, organized as they are in the United States. I do not refer to European systems, because there is such a great disparity between the conditions prevailing on this continent and those prevailing in Europe that comparisons are almost useless to us from the point of view of the establishment of a credit basis for rural people.
Now my hon. friend asks that this resolution be referred to the committee on banking and commerce for further study. While I expect to be fairly busy this session, I would not personally object to that; but surely we should know something of what is in my hon. friend's mind as to the nature of the study to be given to it. For instance, is the committee to call witnesses from the United States to find out how their experiment is getting along? What are we going to do? How are we to get further information? We have available quite a recent report by Doctor Tory, the present head of the National Research Council, which I think is fairly conclusive up to the point of the
2419-20J
commencement of the United States experiment. I have just read the most authentic statement which I can secure from United States sources, that of a committee headed by the present president of the United States, as to the manner in which that experiment is turning out, and I would say that we in Canada would do well to go cautiously with respect to the further development of this matter until we have had a wider experience in the working of our own farm loan scheme and until we have had a longer experience at the expense of our neighbour to the south. AYe know now that the joint stock land bank feature of the United States scheme certainly has not justified the hopes of the promoters. We know that this branch of the United States system is not one which we would desire to bring into effect in this country. As to what weaknesses may develop in connection with the intermediate credit feature, it is too early to say; quite frankly, it is not possible to say, or to gather sufficient information from the limited experience of the United States with intermediate credit institutions upon which to base an opinion.
I do not think there is anything further that I can say at this stage, Mr. Speaker, except to thank my hon. friend for again bringing to the attention of this house a matter which does repay the study put upon it, but for wlhich mankind on this continent has not as yet discovered any royal or guaranteed solution. He expressed it in his resolution, very properly, in very general terms. He speaks of intermediate credit as being a desirable thing, with which statement we could probably all agree, but I do not know whether it is advisable to refer this resolution to the banking and commerce committee unless we have some knowledge of what it is proposed to do with it there.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) has treated this subject so widely and comprehensively that there is not very much left for me to say in the matter, except by way of general discussion of the principle. At the outset he very properly dissociated himself from a supposed class of people who want a great deal of credit disseminated widely among the people. If there is such a class of people I also wish to dissociate myself from them. As a matter of fact, there is no such class of people. That is merely a characterization by those who control credit, of those who seek credit reform. I think it proper for me to make it clear that what is being asked in

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Irvine
the resolution is not more credit but the opportunity for those who may have credit to use it in any manner that may be best for their own interests. In other words, we ask a special credit facility to serve the need of a special agricultural requirement. For those who have no credit, no credit facility is required.
The Minister of Finance in referring to this point very properly said that it is important to have a basis for credit. If there is no basis for credit, of course no one could ask for or get credit, so it is clear that we are not trying to secure for any class of agriculturist something which they do not already have, but rather, as I have said, the right to use what they have. May I point out that in respect to this question the hon. member for Red Deer has set forth a need which he has experienced among his people in the west, a need for the supplying of which I know from personal experience a great many farmers are looking to this house. It is not a creation of his imagination but a real problem perhaps in all agricultural centres throughout Canada, and most decidedly acute in the west.
The question, then, for this house to consider is whether or not that need is there. Not only do I believe such a need exists, but I have recollections of our investigations into credit matters some years ago both in committee and in this house. I recall eminent bankers of this country admitting in committee that there was a need for credit in this connection, that there was what the minister terms a "blank spot" in our credit system, and that this was the blank spot. I think the bankers expressed themselves as being willing to assist in anything that would fill up that gap, and hoped that some means would be found of doing so. I am sure I could mention the names of hon. members of this house, whose influence is unquestionable, who would also agree that there is a need for credit to cover this class of agriculturist.
So the question comes to be one of real practical statesmanship. As the hon. member for Red Deer very properly pointed out the soundness of such a credit business as might result from a consideration of his proposal will depend upon the economic sound-nc:ss of the branches of agriculture in the interests of which such credit facilities would be created. If there is no soundness in these branches of agriculture, the sooner we know it the better.
I do not wish to prolong this debate, but I do want to make a comment on the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). His attitude, in a general way, may be considered

more or less favourable to the general idea, but his attitude of inactivity, as indicated, is not what we had hoped for, nor does it adequately meet the case. He has spoken at some length and in some detail about the sort of organization and machinery which might be considered necessary before such a scheme could be made practicable; he has referred to its working in the United States, pointing out some of its machinery and some of its defects, and has emphasized the fact that the experience so far has not been sufficient to warrant us following their example in every detail. So far so good, but are we to wait without an effort until we know what is going to happen in the working out of the United States system? Does the minister not realize that our farmers are waiting for some assistance in this regard, and it is not sufficient for them to be told that they must wait until the people of the United States have found out how we can be served? That, as I understand it, is the attitude taken by the minister. He says, "We must go cautiously." I agree with him, but in Heaven's name let us go. Let us go somewhere; to go cautiously is not to sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Go where?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Finance who is in charge of this matter and all other matters of credit in Canada, when faced with a definite problem should not be asking me where to go. I presume that, if I were to recognize his question and make an effort to tell him where to go, he would not go very far on my advice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
I should be very glad
to have the hon. member's advice; that is what I am looking for this afternoon.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit this question to go where it can be considered in detail, then if I have any advice I shall be very glad to give it to him and if he treats that advice in the manner he has heretofore I shall not be disappointed. In any case, I will give that advice willingly, but I do say that in his position and with his capabilities, upon which I congratulate him, and convinced as he must be of the actuality of the problem as presented by the hon. member for Red Deer, and also conceding to him the advisability of going cautiously, the minister must see the force of our demand for immediate constructive action.
Before such a need could be met, as has been drawn to the attention of the minister by the hon. member for Red Deer, there must necessarily be a great deal of study, a great deal of investigation and inquiry, and

Agricultural Credits-Mr. McQuarrie
a great deal of organization. That will probably take years to accomplish, but in the meantime are we to sit quietly and do nothing? Can we not study the matter? Can we not investigate it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Surely.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Can we not take some steps towards ultimate action, or are we simply to pass it over and say, "We will wait until the United States have proven that their system is no good, and then, because the United States has failed, we must fail as well. Let us continue therefore, to go so cautiously that we do not go at all."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows
how unfair that is.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
I certainly do not want to
be unfair to the hon. minister, and if my remarks seem to be unfair I want him to know that is the last thought I have in mind. I appreciate the fact that the problem is a very difficult one; I realize also that the minister's task is even more difficult, and I have no desire to say anything which would belittle any opinion which the minister holds. However, I do not think that he himself is satisfied with the answer he made, that we had better not do anything in the meantime. I think we should pass this on to the committee where the matter can be studied. The Minister of Finance asks what is the committee to consider? The reply is that the committee must consider that there is a need for credit facilities to a certain class of agriculturists which are not provided for by the banks or by the Farm Loan Act. The committee should further consider how this parliament can meet that need. As to how far the committee shall go in the calling of witnesses and the extent of the investigation, we leave that to the intelligence of the committee. I would not expect that they should go all over the world for witnesses; I would not even expect that they should go to the United Statees to get people to come here and tell us what not to do. I would rather concentrate on our own problems and peculiar difficulties, and get such men as are available in Canada, without having to go long distances, who could contribute what they know to our consideration of the problem before us. We may not solve the problem this year, or even next year, but that is all the greater reason why we should be busy on it. If it is so intricate, so difficult, the sooner we get on the job the better. I think the minister will find that the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution, and those of us who support him, will be very
reasonable in what we expect the committee to do. We shall not exceed any privilege which may be granted by the passing of the resolution; all we ask for is some action towards the study of the question so that we may not jump into some scheme which may be abortive. I do not think that even I, with all the rashness which my hon. friend attributes to me, would ask him to do anything like that.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer):
That the motion be amended by adding the following words:
"and that this motion be referred to the banking and commerce committee for consideration thereon and report to the house."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject of this
resolution is one which should have full and adequate consideration. There is a blank between the credits furnished by the banks and the credits which are obtainable under the Farm Loan Act; there is an intermediate space which is not being taken care of. As I understand the object of the Farm Loan Act, it was to enable farmers to borrow money with which to carry on and improve their farms, but unfortunately it is not working out that way. I do not intend to criticize in any way the chairman of the board or any of its officers or members-it is the system. The farmer who wants to get money to improve his farm cannot get it from the farm loan board unless he can present securities sufficient to warrant the loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Of course.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
That is to say, he
cannot get money on the farm as it will be after it is improved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
He cannot get money with which to improve his farm or to buy stock; he has to have the same security which he would be required to produce if he were borrowing money from a loan company. I remember the time when loan companies considered farm security as the very best security which could be obtained, and money was freely loaned by loan companies and others on farm lands. I will not attempt to explain to the house the cause, but the fact is that a great many loan companes will not now lend money on farm lands. I have had
310	COMMONS
Agricultural Credits- \Ir. McQuarrie
a number of cases brought to my attention where reputable men who have been farming for many years, men who had every prospect of succeeding, have been unable to borrow money from the farm loan board. No doubt that has been the experience all over the country, because the farm loan board is now taking the place of the loan company in respect to farm loans. That is not a satisfactory condition in a country like Canada, a new country which must be developed and where agriculture is such an important element in our national life, and some means should be devised of advancing money to the man who wishes to improve his farm, provided of course, that it is found after proper investigation that he is a man who is entitled to credit and who in all probability will succeed.
I quite appreciate the fact that there may be some hesitation in lending money on chattel security, and I doubt very much whether it would be fair to urge the banks to lend money on such security. But it seems to me that the whole subject is one which might very well be submitted to the banking and commerce committee without any strings attached to the reference, except the understanding that the committee will be reasonable in making expenditures necessitated by the calling of witnesses and so forth. But I am sure, as was stated by the previous speaker, that that committee may be depended upon not to do anything unreasonable. The [DOT]Canadian farmer should be helped. I know what the situation is in British Columbia. ~SYe have good land in that province, but in many cases we have first to remove the trees and stumps before the land can be cultivated. How is the farmer going to do that unless he gets some kind of assistance? As far as I can see one of the responsibilities of the government of the Dominion is to assist the agriculturists so that Canada can be developed as it should be.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
A few moments ago I asked the minister a question, and I fear he had not the information under his hand to answer it. It, however, to my mind bears directly upon this resolution, and it ought to be considered really before any action is taken on the resolution itself. In order to make my question clearer to the minister's mind, may I recall to his memory and to the memory of the mover of the resolution and other hon. gentlemen present what has already occurred in parliament? In 1923 parliament spent, I think, some three months in revising the Bank Act. .During the revision of the Bank Act, which

was perhaps one of the most seriously considered revisions in the history of Canada, one thing that stood out very clearly was the inadequacy of provision in the banking system of Canada to meet the needs of the agriculturist of the country, that is, something of a nature other than on strictly banking principles. I recall very well my hon. friend who has moved the resolution (Mr. Speak-man), the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), several other hon. gentlemen and myself were on a subcommittee, I think the subsequent session, to consider that particular phase of the question and difficulty. That committee brought in a report which I find referred to in Dr. Tory's report dealing with the question. In other words, it was recognized that there was a hiatus which was not bridged by the Bank Act. The subcommittee recommended-and the banking and commerce committee accepted their recommendation and the house accepted it-that some steps should be taken. The committee recommended as follows:
Therefore, your committee recommend that the investigation of the subject-
That is really the same subject that we are talking about now.
-he continued in order to determine whether it be possible to coordinate the various systems of rural credit now in existence into a federal system applicable to the whole of Canada, and that legislation be prepared based on the said further investigations and calculated to meet the credit needs of the agricultural classes of the Dominion, and submitted to parliament at its next session.
Fallowing that, Dr. Tory was appointed as a commission or commissioner to make an investigation. He presented two reports, one in 1924 and his final report in 1925. I have had these under my hand only for a moment or two, and I have not had time to go into them to any greater extent than to refresh my memory, but I would like to call attention to one or two points in that report because, after all, I find very frequently parliament repeats over and over again work it has already done. In this report Dr. Tory makes certain observations. For instance, he has on page 18 of the final report some observations regarding intermediate credits, the very subject that is being discussed this afternoon. He says:
The period of intermediate loans varies from six months to three years, depending somewhat on the punpose to which the money is to be applied. It is a banking operation, although it may have associated with it a chattel mortgage as security. Generally, the security is personal, or non-perishable farm products, or live stock.

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Stevens
Then he says that certain methods may be brought in regarding it. He says that there is cooperation-, government assistance, or a combination of the two. Then he goes on to say:
I am of the opinion that the road to the solution of the problem for Canada lies in another direction.
Then he makes this statement:
I think that experience has already shown that a sound plan along these lines could be worked out under proper supervision and control. It would be a definite step toward the realization ultimately of financial control and, therefore, independence by the farmers themselves. Discounting facilities would have to be provided by some central agency, either a corporation specially created, as suggested by the president of the Bank of Commerce, or organized and to some extent at least, capitalized by the government, as in the United States.
Then he says:
Two methods of meeting the difficulty are suggested:
(a)	Through the development further of cooperative organizations;
(b)	Through provincial savings banks.
Then ihe says:
I am of the opinion that the development of cooperative organizations is the proper way to proceed, and for the following reasons:
(1)	It will give the farmer himself the experience which will teach him how to use money advantageously and in a business way;
(2)	It will, if successful, lead ultimately to financial independence by putting him in relation to a self-supporting financial institution through which capital can be commanded.
He goes on ,to say:
I am further of the opinion that the organization, supervision and control of this type of credit should be left to the provinces. Dominion supervision would be difficult and expensive.
There follow some other observations of an equally interesting character. Following that report, the government of which my hon. friend is a member, and I may say through his late predecessor whom I am exceedingly sorry to note has passed from our midst, introduced an act called an act for the purpose of establishing in Canada a system of long term mortgage credit for farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Canadian Farm Loan Act is the title.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Yes, the short title. What I wish to draw the attention of the house to is this: when -that act was brought down, it was stated very clearly by the government-* and it has been so argued before the agricultural public of the country-that it was introduced to carry out the recommendations of the banking and commerce committee to which I have referred, and the recommendations of Dr. Tory who made an exhaustive investigation and an excellent report. But as a matter of fact, as the minister himself argued when I asked my question of him a few minutes ago, the Farm Loan Act apparently is not doing that. That is the point I wanted to find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: It is not an intermediate credit act.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: No; but the point was that the government introduced it as an intermediate loan act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Unquestionably the government brought it into the house as a solution of the problem to which I have been referring in connection with these reports. My hon. friend (Mr. Spencer) will recall perfectly well that it was the rural credits or intermediate credits we argued about for months in the banking and commerce committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: I know my hon. friend does not want to be unfair in the matter. It fell to my lot, substituting for my late friend, Mr. Robb, to pilot 'that measure through the committee stage in the house, and I certainly remember drawing a clear distinction at all times between the two problems of long-term mortgage credits and intermediate credits. I certainly never attempted to convey to anyone that this was an effort to deal with the intermediate credit feature of the problem.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
What the minister says may be perfectly true; I am not disputing that at all, but what I do say is that the problem of intermediate credits for agriculture has been before this house for the last fen years. It has been actively before this house since 1923, and we have spent a great deal of time studying the problem. Doctor Tory's report deals specifically with it. The point I am making at the moment is that in producing the Farm Loan Act this government did not discharge its duty in regard to the report which its own commissioner made.
I turn to the act itself. I have not had time to peruse it very carefully, but from a hasty survey one or two points arise to which I would like to refer.
In connection with loans, it certainly does provide that they must be a first mortgage

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Stevens
security on the farm, and that the proceeds of such loans shall be used for the following purposes:
(i)	To purchase farm land; (ii) To purchase fertilizers, seed, live stock, tools, machinery and any implements and equipment necessary to the proper operation of the farm mortgaged; (iii) To erect farm buildings or to clear, drain, fence or make any other permanent improvement tending to increase the productive value of the land; (iv) To discharge liabilities already accumulated.
That is a pretty broad provision. It continues :
(v) Any purpose which in the judgment of the board may be reasonably considered as improving the value of the land for agricultural purposes.
It is true that this act is not called an intermediate credit loans act, but it is a pretty wide measure and provides for a broad distribution and use of the funds, and as a matter of fact it fairly well covers almost everything the farmer would require. My hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) calls my attention to the fact that paragraph (b) of section 7 of the act refers specifically to live stock. I will read that paragraph again:
(ii)	To purchase fertilizers, seed, live stock, tools, machinery and any implements and equipment necessary to the proper operation of the farm mortgaged.
The minister raised the question a few moments ago that the act was in fact a long term act, whatever it might be called. Here is what paragraph (h) of section 7 says:
_ Notwithstanding anything in this act, but subject to such regulations as the board may prescribe not inconsistent with the provisions of the Interest Act, any borrower may at any time repay the whole or any part thereof on any date on which an instalment becomes due, and any such payment shall be credited to the borrower in such manner as the board may by regulation prescribe as hereinafter provided, but no such payment shall relieve the borrower from meeting all subsequent payments punctually as they fall due.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Does not that clause make it a short term loan?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Absolutely. They can borrow the money to-day and repay it in six months. The instalments become due every six months and the whole loan may be paid off on any date when the instalments become due.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: My hon. friend is a student of these matters, I know, but I am sure he would not suggest that for a live stock loan a farmer should go to the expense of putting a mortgage on his land, with all that is involved in that.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: Certainly not, but this act was palmed off on the country as meeting the requirements which we are now discussing.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext: My hon. friend says "no, no," but I would remind him and the rest of the house of the weeks and months that we spent in the banking and commerce committee in different years discussing this very question.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
I was a
member of the committee.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR INTRODUCTION OF SYSTEM OF INTERMEDIATE FARM LOANS
speechtext:
Yes, and my hon. friend
from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) was a member of the subcommittee, and this subject of intermediate credits was the whole subject of our discussions, other than the revision of the Bank Act; and for three years this very subject was discussed. My submission is this, that in this report of Doctor Toiy you have all the information you require at the present time, and if you have not, I can refer the house to evidence, a pile four feet high, which you will find in the custody of the clerk of the banking and commerce committee, taken from representatives from all over the United States and Canada and from societies interested in this matter. There are piles-I was going to say tons-of evidence on this subject, and the point I am making is that with all this evidence available, together with the report of Doctor Tory, the government is in just as good a position to bring down an act now to meet the situation as it would be if we spent more time this session going over the whole question again and collecting more evidence. I recall, or I am almost certain, that when this act was passing through the house I pointed out to the government that it did not meet completely the requirements of the report of Doctor Toiry, but I said that as it went part of the way I had no particular objections to it. speechtext:
This question, Mr. Speaker, has become acute of late years, and while I should like to see the whole question of agricultural credits again investigated by a special committee of this house, I do think the government should have acted on the findings of the special committee on agriculture made about five years ago. There is a cause for this question having become acute at the present time. First, the banks are not giving the farmers adequate credit to carry on their operations. Now, why are they not lending? The fact is the security is not sufficient. A good many years ago the banks loaned very freely, at least for three, six or nine months in the year; now they are not doing so. In some cases the farmers to whom they made loans have become so involved that the banks themselves have had to take over the farms. I have in mind one or two cases where farmers were induced to borrow money for the sake of increasing their production. To-day the banks own the farms. In one case on an eight hundred acre farm ten thousand dollars was borrowed. Later the bank secured title to the farm. Then they sold it to another farmer, who paid a substantial sum of money down. He himself to-day is in the same pickle as the former owner-in debt to such an extent that he can never hope to clear himself.
It seems to me that if the government had acted on the findings of the special committee on agriculture of five years ago we would have somewhat solved this problem by now. The main cause of the whole trouble is that the prices of farm products are out of line entirely with the prices of what the farmer has got to purchase. We are told we should raise more live stock, and I believe that next week in this city a conference will be held under the auspices of the Department of Agriculture to consider increasing the production of farm products for export. As I say, the prices of everything produced on the farm are out of line entirely with what the farmer needs to carry on his operations. Even the milled stuffs with which he feeds his stock are dearer to-day in western Canada than they are in any of the countries to which our farm products are being shipped. For this reason the banks do not feel that sufficient security is offered for the credit required.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has said that local conditions do not lend themselves to the organization of local credit societies. This is only too true, because farming in a manner has become a precarious occupation. To-day our farm population is moving to the urban centres, and indeed we are changing more and more from the landlord class to the tenant class. Towards the end of the war the banks loaned freely for the production of live stock, but they did not give sufficient time to the farmer to realize on his live stock, and many of those men today have been forced off the land. That we need credit is no doubt plain to all, but we should strike at the root cause of the problem. For this reason I should like to see the whole question investigated by a special committee of this house, with power to bring before them all those concerned in credit operations, loan companies and so on, and I think this would be the best course to take at the present time.
