Mr. Speaker, before the question is put there are one or two points which we might clear up. I must first of all congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on being back again with us, and also thank him most heartily for the intense cooperation and earnest work that he has always extended to his colleagues in this house in connection with this question. I think the hon. gentleman and Sir Henry Drayton were the two members of the Conservative party sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, who were the most interested and certainly did the most work in this regard. I do not think there is any member in the house who has more consistently or more earnestly devoted his ability to the solution of the problem that is before us than the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
In his speech a few moments ago he referred to the undoubted fact that for nearly three years the banking committee had considered the problem of intermediate credits. It did so, but it considered intermediate credits only as one phase of the problem of agricultural credits. When this federal legislation to which reference has been made, known as the Canadian Farm Loan Act, was introduced no gold brick was handed to me, nor do I think the agricultural class of western Canada were in the least deluded as to what they got. It is true the expectations aroused at that time have not been met. But they never expected the long term loan act

Agricultural Credits-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
to mean an intermediate credit act. At no time could that statement be made as one of fact. There may have been individuals who confused the two questions. I do not recollect a single paragraph in Dr. Tory's report where he made any specific recommendation to parliament in the matter of intermediate credits- not a single one. The specific recommendations leading towards legislation dealt almost entirely with a long term rural credit system. I shall not at the moment discuss in detail the long term rural credit system, but it may not be amiss to say, in passing, that it is not meeting the requirements of agriculture. It is, on the whole, being administered in a most unsatisfactory manner. Possibly the reason for that is undue cautiousness on the part of the provincial officers who have the administrative responsibility in connection with the assessment and granting of loans. Whatever the reasons are, agriculture as a whole is not satisfied with the working out of the present act. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) quoted from the act itself to show that loans might be made for the purposes of live stock, improvement of the farm, seed grain, machinery, and other things. That is all true, but no farmer wants to ask a long term loan for the purpose of making a short term commitment or investment. No business man would want to do it, and no farmer wants to do it. The difficulty in connection with that is that before you can get a loan under this act you have to undertake the expense of the inspection and the assessment, and all the other burdens of cost that are common to the issuing of a loan on a mortgage. A loan is made, not on the basis of chattel goods but on the basis of the land itself with a small percentatge for improvements to the permanent buildings on the farm. A farmer, therefore, is not going to borrow money for live stock investment, for the purchase of seed, or things of that kind, under an act such as we now have. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the intermediate needs of agriculture are not being met by this act, and whether or not the hon. member for Vancouver Centre or any other hon. member has the conception that the act was to meet that need does not really matter at the moment. The fact is the need is present, and therefore the hon. member for Red Deer may well be congratulated for asking that the house consider this question, and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) should also be congratulated for suggesting the very reasonable procedure that the question should again be referred to the banking and commerce committee, the only body over
which we have jurisdiction in this house that can give sufficiently intelligent consideration to the question, and the only body that could recommend back to this house legislation which would meet the immediate requirements of agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, the present banking system has much to recommend it to commercial institutions, but so far as agriculture is concerned, any service that we have secured-and there is no question the system has been of service to us-has been rather because of the generosity of the bankers than because of the Bank Act or the provisions under the Bank Act. If in the beginning of the year a farmer wants a loan of money, varying from S200 to $10,000, for his current requirements, he goes to the local branch manager and presents his case. The local branch manager pulls out a drawer, takes therefrom a long piece of paper, and proceeds to put the farmer through a catechism as intense as that to which a person is subjected when he goes to hospital. After you get through with the local bank manager you feel that he has on that piece of paper your life history, your family's life history and everything belonging to you. That is all right; he is making an estimate of your financial condition, and after it is all over he grants you the loan. In the old days in western Canada very little difficulty was experienced in getting a small loan for current purposes. The west has been built up on credit-it is true it was its own credit- extended to it by banks that became established out there. Well, the farmer gets that loan for three months. At the time the loan is made, both the banker who makes it and the farmer who gets it know that it cannot and will not be repaid in three months. There is the peculiar situation about it all. Although it is a loan for three months at eight per cent-and we do not get money any cheaper out there even now-the banker knows the farmer could not pay in three months. The three months elapse. The loan, we will say, was taken out in April. April, May and June have gone by, and the middle of July is here. The farmer gets a note from the banker saying, "Your note is due, come in and see me." The farmer goes in and interviews the banker. By this time the banker has got a message from head office telling him to cut down on his loans, telling him that times are bad, or that money is more stringent. The banker asks the farmer if he can at least pay the interest on his note. The farmer tells him he cannot because he has not liquidated any stock in the meantime, and he has not got the wheat and will not
316	COMMONS
Agricultural Credits-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
have it bill the crop is harvested. Under the Bank Act, banks are not permitted to lend money on real estate, but as soon as the farmer goes in he asks for a renewal of his note. The banker then asks if he has a mortgage on his land, and if the farmer tells him he has not he will ask him to bring in his title; so that in effect the money is actually loaned on real estate, because it is then held as collateral three months later. Just about a month after that harvest comes on, and the farmer has to have more money, harvest expenses are usually cash-binder twine, labour, and so on. The farmer requires another S200. Of course the manager is getting nervous-that is, if he has been left there long enough-and he will tell you that he will take the matter up with his superintendent, who may be anywhere from four hundred to two thousand miles away. He takes it up with his superintendent. You go in to see him a week later and he tells you, "Well, frankly, I have taken the matter up but things are not looking very good; crop conditions are bad,"-or that the farmer has too much wheat, or the price is low, or there is something wrong. He says: "Have you any cattle?" and if you admit having some cattle he will ask you if you would mind giving their description, age and brand marks

"on this piece of paper, thank you," -and then you sign that. It is a chattel mortgage on the cattle. Now, Mr. Speaker, I make the assertion, without fear of contradiction, that if the Canadian 'bankers ever lost a dollar in western Canada it was not through any fault of theirs; it was through conditions over which they had no personal control, or conditions which could not have been foreseen. That banking system, to any member who is a farmer, and to those who are studying the question, is obviously wholly unsuited for the mixed farming which we are advised now to take up. The farmer is continually being told: "You have to stop this straight grain raising and go into mixed farming if you want to be prosperous and thrifty."
I do not think anybody has been deluded as to the purposes of the long term rural credits act which passed the house in 1926. It may be that in time, under good administration, with improved methods of assessment, and so on, the working of the act may be improved. At the present time it is not working satisfactorily. Even if it were working splendidly, even if long term loans were available freely and easily to those who deserve or require them, still the act would not take the place of that which the hon. member for Red Deer is requesting. I strongly support the resolution, Mr. Speaker, and I trust 
that this house will see the wisdom of referring once more to a committee the consideration of this problem so tlhat we may try to do something, not five or six years hence but as soon as possible, to meet the intermediate requirements of agriculture. I can readily understand and sympathize with the point of view of the Minister of Finance. The country is sparsely settled. The problems of intermediate credits are problems that are intensified by sparse settlement, by lack of intensive agricultural developments and by lack of immediately .available markets. Our system of agriculture in Canada is undergoing a steady .change, the rapidity and healthiness of which may depend largely upon the character of itlhe credit system which we may institute.
The minister suggested that he would like to have some idea as to the direction in which we were tending in regard to this system of intermediate credits. I want to say to him quite frankly that the only form of such credits I can conceive at the moment as being practical and applicable to western Canada would be a system based upon the establishment of local cooperative rural credit secieties where, so far as may be possible, you will get pooled together the credit resources of zones, districts or even of provinces. The smaller you start of course the weaker the system will be; the larger the unit the stronger the system, but I take it that we will have to start in a small way at first. In my own province we have a small cooperative system in operation which would at once interlock with any federal scheme of cooperative rural credits, and I should like to see the committee investigate this question along those lines.
With that statement, Mr. Speaker, I give my support to this motion, sincererly trusting that the house will see the wisdom of referring this question to the committee.

I think it fair to say, without casting any reflection on any province, that the provincial schemes cannot be regarded as having been successful in meeting the problem of intermediate credits, and so I suggest that the committee might welt endeavour to get at the causes which have occasioned the disappointment which has been experienced with regard to these provincial schemes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to be very brief in what I have to say. First I wish to thank those members, and particularly the Minister of Finance, who have taken part in the debate, for the interest shown in and the sympathetic consideration given to this resolution. .
In advancing this suggestion I purposely refrained from advocating any definite or specific manner of approaching this work or of setting up any system of intermediate credits. My purpose in so doing must be obvious. I have taken the trouble to study to some degree the different systems in vogue in different places, and I agree with the Minister of Finance that none has proved completely successful. Many difficulties have occurred in the development of the work, and the operation of the greater number of these systems leaves some doubt as to the best method to pursue. With that in mind, together with the fact that I was unable to evolve any system satisfactory to myself, I wished to leave the matter entirely open. I trusted that the committee would not undertake to go over the work covered in past years, during the progress of which a great amount of very useful evidence was collected, but that it might continue the work in the hope of finding some solution based upon that and any further evidence which might be found available at the present time. I do trust that the committee will not only examine the systems which have shown signs of success, but will also pay particular attention to the weaknesses which may have developed and the difficulties which may have arisen. While I am extremely anxious that such a system should bo put into operation with the least possible delay, I am even more anxious that this system when set up may function satisfactorily. In respect to the possibilities under the present long term
318	COMMONS
Agricultural Credits-Mr. Speakman
legislation, like the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) I am under no illusion as to its application to farm credit. In addition to the various difficulties which have been suggested already, I have only to point out that under the terms of the Canadian Farm Loan Act, no credit is available to homesteaders or renters; it is confined to those who have a clear title to their land. No man in the process of purchasing a farm or developing a homestead-there are thousands in that condition and we hope to have thousands more-can make use of the provisions ot the present act, even though he were prepared to undergo the trouble and stand the expense of applying for a loan.
This problem presents a definite field of endeavour to the banking and commerce committee, of which I am sorry to say I am no longer a member, and I am prepared to trust them to make a real examination of the circumstances and to give a sympathetic and interested study of the problem. I am quits prepared also to trust that committee to be reasonable in their demands upon the public exchequer.
I realize that this is a tremendously involved question, and if I may repeat what I have said before-I repeat it for the purpose of emphasis, not for mere reiteration-it is infinitely more essential to be certain of every step taken, to make as few mistakes as possible, to ascertain that we are on the right road before we start, then to plunge into it in too big a hurry. I am as anxious to see it put into effect as soon as possible as any hon. member in the house, I realize the need and the necessity of the farmers of this country for such a measure, but I am quite sure I am speaking for the common sense of those farmers when I say that they want something which will be based upon sound business administration and which will function as credit should function, to enable them to carry on business in a satisfactory way and not merely cause them to accumulate indebtedness which eventually would prove their ruin.
May I thank the minister and the other members of the house for their sympathetic acceptance of this resolution, and may I again say that I trust we may find a solution to this problem, and in so doing take a further step in bringing the agricultural industry of Canada to the place it should occupy.

I should not have asked that scholarships be instituted in each Canadian university, because I am addressing myself only to the general principle that the federal government has a responsibility in regard to education for peace.

I had the belief that there were some seventeen universities in Canada, but the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) said the other day that there were twenty-three. I do not know which figure is correct, but seventeen universities would be sufficient for the object I have in mind, in fact more than sufficient. Supposing we started with seventeen universities-

If we allowed $6,000

International Peace-Miss Macphail
The fact that this parliament last year ratified the Kellogg pact, and -that -the leader of the delegation to Geneva this year signed the optional clause in the name of Canada convinces me that the Canadian people are desirous of obtaining peace through peaceful methods. They want peace and they are willing to adopt measures which they think will bring it about. Neither the people in Canada nor the people of other countries have as yet worked out a technique of peace. I was interested in reading an article entitled The New Patriotism is Peace by Mrs. Sinclair Lewis. This article appeared in the Readers Digest of 1930, and is a condensation of the original article in the Pictorial Review of December 1929. In making the point that we have not yet addressed ourselves to the technique of peace she said:
We must face the fact that to avert war we shall have to throw overboard a whole system of old ideas. It is a striking fact that the League of Nations, with all its secretariats, bureaus and commissions, could run for 600 years on the military budgets of its members for a single year. All of tradition is still on the side of war.
And that is true in Canada as in other countries. Still. I believe the Canadian people have lost confidence in armaments as a means to security and we are now at -the place where we are willing to try another method. We are willing to try to get peace by preparing for it, not to get peace by preparing for war, as was the old idea. It is because I believe we have reached the point where we are willing to consider new ideas that I have proposed this resolution and submitted it to the house for its approval.
I think we shall all admit that the world is an economic unit. This is a fact but it is not one that is generally recognized or realized. In Canada particularly we have been so lately drawn into world currents that we still suffer from narrowness and localism and it seems to me that the best approach to internationalizing the ideas and outlook of our Canadian people would be through our universities. The young people who go out from the universities with a properly developed foreign sense, as I would expect they would, should they come under the influence of a department of national affairs, would little by little diffuse that sense through the communities in which they live and they would help very materially to create and maintain in Canada an informed and intelligent opinion on foreign affairs. I believe Canada has a part to play in foreign affairs, a part that will become increasingly greater because we are still a young country
and because of our size from a geographical point of view. Our population is still sparse and our entrance into international affairs has only recently taken place, so that our place in the world is destined to become greater as the years go by. Already, however, Canada has .a considerable place in foreign affairs. We have now for a year or two had a place on the council of the League of Nations. We have established two legations, one in Washington and one in Japan. We have representatives-I may not be using the correct terms -in Geneva, Paris and London, and the work that is carried on in all of those places requires, and as time goes on will to a greater extent require, the services of young men and women who are well fitted to -take their place there. Those young men and women can be well fitted to do so only if they have a knowledge of international affairs. They must be definitely trained to serve in our offices abroad, whether we call them legations or the offices of representatives. It would seem to me it would be wise that as large a number as possible of these young men and women who gc to serve abroad should first have had experience in the Department of External Affairs ai home. They need to know the conditions thai we have to meet right here in Canada; thej need to know something about the personali ties they must work with in the home office when they go abroad. I should like to ask the government and, indeed, all of us:	What
provision have any of us tried to make for young people that they may fit themselves for service abroad? I wonder whether there is any other country as badly equipped to fit their young men and women to serve us well when they go to represent us in other parts of the world. Very few of our universities are equipped with departments of international affairs. I do not think there are any that are equipped with a department under that name. I believe Toronto university has a department of international law headed by Professor Mackenzie.
The government has in the past been able to find money to promote research in other fields such as agriculture, forestry and science, and it would seem to me that such a fundamental question as the maintenance of peace is worthy of consideration and action. I anticipate from other debates that we have had in the house on similar subjects, that some member of the government, if they bother to reply to the resolution, will say: But education is a provincial matter and we cannot interfere with it. I would recognize that in my sleep;

International Peace-Miss Macphail
I have heard it so often from the treasury benches that I know that is their stock-intrade reply. I notice, too, when the government of the Dominion wants to interfere, if that word is not objectionable, with education in the provinces, they are always able to do so. The Department of National Defence gives rather large sums in grants each year to schools throughout the different provinces to promote education for war. If we can interfere with education to promote ideas that will, if carried to their ultimate conclusion, lead to war, I see no reason why *ve cannot interfere with education to promote ideas that, if followed, will lead to peace. I think parliament has voted sums of money for technical education in the different provinces, so I am not asking for the first time that we should give sums of money in grants to the provinces. We have done it twice before: first to promote war, and, second, to promote a better understanding of technical things, so I feel the third time is not too much. Then, too, the question of peace and war is a federal matter. It is the business of the Dominion government to see to matters of peace and war, and if they are to see to the carrying out of war, is it not logical that they should strive by educational means to avoid war which we have found to be very costly? If we leave this matter to the initiative of the provinces, the most forward-looking of the provinces are most likely to take action on it first and they, I might say, are the provinces that need it least. If the grant is given at the same time to all the provinces, it will tend to maintain a uniformity of ideas throughout Canada and there is enough difference between ideas in the provinces already without adding to it.
In Canada we need a department of international affairs in the universities more than it is needed in most countries. In Great Britain, for instance, they have many great societies that have for their object the promotion of peace through the dissemination of knowledge in regard to foreign affairs. For example, in Great Britain the Foreign Office has a section that is devoted exclusively to the affairs of the League of Nations. That section of the Foreign Office is headed by a most capable man and he has many assistants. They devote their whole time to the affairs of the ieague, and through that office and through the association of the League of Nations a great deal of knowledge is disseminated throughout Great Britain and made available to the people. They do that to a much greater extent than we do here where
(Miss Macphail.3
an overburdened man has charge of affairs pertaining to the league. In Great Britain they have a large organization called the National Council for the Prevention of War. Hon. members may or may not be familiar with its work, but it is excellent; it is of a high character and it is educational. The Union of Democratic Control was started a long time ago, one of the founders being Ramsay MacDonald, now Prime Minister of Great Britain, and there is published by that organization an excellent magazine called Foreign Affairs. That magazine is read, I believe, by many hon. members and we know how excellent it is.
While the government of the United States, one would sometimes think, is not very much affected by public opinion in that country, still they have there some splendid organizations for the promotion of peace through education. Among the best is the National Council for the Prevention of War, the secretary of which is Frederick Libby of Washington, but they have many others and they have some worthwhile magazines: Current History, which is familiar to us all, the World To-morrow, Foreign Affairs, and The Nation, which to some extent devotes itself to international affairs. In Canada we are particularly lacking in an organization that has for its object the promoting of peace through educational methods. We have almost nothing at all. There are the League of Nations' associations. There are three sections, I think, of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom, and I am afraid that is about all. It is true that the Women's Christian Temperance Union, feeling I suppose that temperance was for the moment a lost cause, have to a great extent taken up this work of peace. There are no others that I know' of. We have absolutely no magazine, except one published by the League of Nations in this city, that has for its object the promoting of peace through education.

I think we will all admit, too, that the Rhodes scholarships did very much for the welding together of the different parts of the empire, and what the Rhodes scholarships did for the British commonwealth I believe that international scholarships would do for the world. Of course, we could not do it by ourselves alone, but if all the nations made a practice of
